opener.heading: Week 39: Letters & Sounds 🔤
about: AZLYN is five letters and she gets all five every day, in a new material each time. Friday they go up the hall wall in poster paint at her height, hers to walk past. Saturday they are card strips and paper-plate curves on a baking tray, and Sunday she throws sock balls at them until the clothespins run out. Wednesday you cut her name apart and she puts it back together. Thursday she rolls the letters out of shortbread dough. You say the sound every time and never the letter name, so that by Sunday she can find her own door in the hall.

No holiday lands this week. Late September does the work instead: buckeyes under the horse chestnut, the first real leaf fall, fence wood damp enough to hold a water letter for a minute, and spider webs strung across every gate. Chalk goes out with you on Friday and again on Sunday. Tuesday she spends painted as whichever animal she picks, and Thursday finishes with three wrapped cookies in a tin on a high shelf and a girl checking it every ten minutes until six.
azlyn: The five letters of her own name. She paints them, jumps them, throws at them and eats one, and the shape holds across all five.
Sounds instead of letter names. Sss for the s and zzz for the z, which is the version she needs when she comes to read a word.
Which way round a letter faces. One straight strip and one curve make b, d, p and q, and she is the one moving the curve.
Aim, from repetition. Twenty throws at a wall of letters, then five holes cut in a box, and no coaching between throws.
Holding on to three cookies until six o'clock. She wraps them, ties them and puts them out of her own reach, then hands them over at the table.
you: Jumping is a year-old skill by now, and distance is the part still arriving
"Different" and "wrong" are separate ideas, and this week teaches the difference
Aiming improves with quantity, not instruction
Risk and reward is a new kind of decision
A painted face changes behavior as well as appearance
Building it back up is the part that's doing the work
Saving three of something is harder than it sounds
shopping: Cereal boxes, 6 (five to flatten, one to cut into strips)
Food boxes out of the cabinet, 6, with letters big enough to circle
Plain paper, a stack of letter-size
Permanent markers, 2, one of them thick
Thick card, 1 sheet, for September's handprint
Washable non-toxic poster paint, 1 color, for September's handprint
A small soft brush, or a handful of cotton swabs
The widest brush in the house, for the fence
A craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Poster putty, 1 pack, or a lump of playdough
Baking trays, 2 (one as a work surface, one for the cookies)
A plate, for the dough in the fridge
Paper bags, 2, or a tote for the postbag
Old socks you don't want back, 5
A large cardboard box, the biggest you have
A tin or box with a lid
Twelve household objects, fist-sized or bigger
A jump rope or a bathrobe cord
Store-bought face paints, if you have them
An old T-shirt she can ruin
Three or four of her own books
All-purpose flour, 2 cups (250 g), plus extra for the board
Butter, 1½ sticks (175 g), out to soften on Wednesday night
A cup, for Kreston at the fence
Rolled oats, or a tub of peas to defrost, for the duck pond
Rice and sesame seeds, for Friday's dinner
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 15 months this week. He runs, spoons his own food, and points at pictures in books, which this week is a tool. Name whatever his finger lands on, then say its first sound on its own, and he gets the week's lesson without any of the work.

days.title: The Letters in Her Name
days.prepTonight: Flatten five cereal boxes, stack them by the poster paint, and leave six food boxes out on the counter for the morning.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Her Letters on the Cereal Boxes

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Her Name, Big Enough to Stand On

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Book With Her Name In It

opening.title: Her Letters on the Cereal Boxes
opening.need: 6 food boxes · 1 thick permanent marker · 1 strip of paper.
steps: Write AZLYN along the strip in capitals, stand it in front of her and push the boxes into the middle of the table.
Point at the A on her strip and hunt for an A on a box. Circle it with the marker, then hand the marker to her.
Work through the Z, the L, the Y and the N. Leave the five circled boxes standing. You paint those letters at 9:15.

main.title: Her Name, Big Enough to Stand On
materials: 5 flattened cereal boxes or cardboard sheets
The circled boxes from the opening, as models
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Lay the five sheets on the floor. Draw one letter on each in marker, corner to corner, as big as the card takes.
Stand the matching box beside each sheet so she looks from the small letter to the huge one.
Give her the brush and the first color. She paints along your lines and outside them. Leave it.
Second color once the first is on. She decides where it goes.
Washcloth between colors, or both turn brown by the third letter.
Once dry, tape the five along the hall wall in order at her height. Walk her past with her finger on each and say the sounds, ah, zz, ll, ih, nn.
main.tip: Sounds, not letter names. Zee and why are names she has to unlearn before she can read her own off the wall.

outside.title: Jumping the Name Path
paras: Take a fat stick of sidewalk chalk to a path set back from the road. Chalk her five letters in a line, a stride apart, and let her jump from each to the next saying the sound as she lands. Then backwards, then on one foot, which she falls over doing. Late September damp helps: chalk takes better on wet stone, and the line washes off in the next rain.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at pictures in books. Give him his own stub of chalk on the path and let him press it flat against the stone beside her line. He holds it in a fist and leans his whole weight on it.

second.title: A Letter for Every Door
second.intro: Four people live here and four doors have nothing on them.
materials: 4 sheets of thick card or cereal-box card
6 sheets of paper for the drawings
1 paper bag or tote as the postbag
steps: Ask her who lives in this house. Take the four names as she gives them and write the first letter of each big on a sheet of card: B, J, A, K.
She fills them in with crayons. Say whose is whose while she works.
Tape each to that person's door at her height, not yours. She has to be able to touch it.
Walk the house once and read the doors out. Ask her to find the one that is hers.
Six sheets of paper and the crayons. She draws for whoever she likes. Ask who each one is for and write the name on the back.
Load the postbag and send her off. She matches the drawing in her hand to the letter on the door.
Leave the four letters up all week. She will be reading her own door by Sunday.
second.tip: She will post to the wrong door. Do not correct it. Ask her to say the letter on the door out loud and she hears the mismatch before you name it.

alternatives: One letter only, hers, on her own door.
Draw round her hand on card and turn it into an A.
Mail the drawings under the doors instead.
Label the kitchen drawers instead of the doors.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, and let her tell them what her name starts with
The playground, with a sleeve for drying the slide
A walk hunting her letters on license plates and vans
The corner store, and she finds one A on the shelf
Home to the leaf pile if the rain comes in

aroundWorld.title: Korea: Hangul 🇰🇷
paras: Most alphabets grew by accident over centuries. Korea's was designed on purpose. In the 1440s King Sejong set scholars to build a writing system ordinary people could learn in a morning, and the letter shapes show where the tongue and lips go to make each sound. Twenty-four letters, stacked into a neat block for every syllable.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Arrange a bowl of rice at dinner the way bibimbap is arranged, each thing in its own section, and lay her initial across the top in sesame seeds. She eats her own letter.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: South Korea keeps a public holiday for its alphabet, Hangul Day, on the ninth of October.

days.krestonPM: Give him a spare sheet of card and one crayon at the low table while she colors the door letters. At 15 months he runs, so hand him a finished drawing, point at the door it belongs to, and let him carry it there.

insight.headline: Jumping is a year-old skill by now, and distance is the part still arriving.
paras: Azlyn has been leaving the ground with both feet at once, on purpose, since some months after her second birthday, and what she has today is a short hop forward. The jump asks her to push off both legs in the same instant, hold her body in the air with nothing under it, and land without her knees folding. Length is the piece that keeps building, across this whole year and the next one. Giving her something to land on buys you twenty repetitions where jump for me buys three, and she gets the letter practice as a side effect of wanting to land on the Z.

days.safety: Chalk letters on a sidewalk put her head down and her feet moving near a curb. Pick a path set back from the road, chalk the run parallel to it rather than towards it, and keep Kreston in the stroller or holding a hand while she jumps. The permanent marker goes back on a high shelf between uses. At 15 months he is fast, and it is the right size for his mouth.

days.title: Which Way Round
days.prepTonight: Cut twelve finger-long strips from a cereal box and six curves from a paper plate, leave them on the baking tray with the poster putty, and put the scissors away.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Alphabet You Lie Down In

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Photos From the Floor

opening.title: Two Sticks and a Curve
opening.need: 2 card strips · 2 paper-plate curves · poster putty · 1 baking tray.
steps: Stand a strip upright on the tray with a pea of poster putty under it and press a curve against its bottom right. That is a b. Say the sound.
Hand her a strip and a curve and let her copy it beside yours.
Move your curve to the bottom left of your own strip and say nothing. Ask whether it is still a b, and leave the question open until 9:15.

main.title: Making b Into d
materials: 12 straight strips cut from cereal-box card, roughly a finger long
6 curves cut from a paper plate
1 lump of playdough or a pack of poster putty
1 baking tray as the work surface
Her name written out on a strip of paper as the model
steps: Write AZLYN along the paper strip in marker and lay it across the top of the tray. She builds the A, Z, L and N below it from straight strips, a pinch of poster putty under each.
Add a curve. One strip standing tall, one curve at its bottom right: b. Say the sound.
Lift the curve off and press it to the bottom left of the same strip: d. Let her flip it back and forth.
Slide the strip down so it hangs below the curve. That is a p, and moving the curve across makes a q.
Call a letter and let her build it. Get one wrong on purpose and wait for her to spot it, which she will, at volume.
Finish on her own initial. Three strips, an A at the top of the tray, and it stays there.
main.tip: She will build a backwards N and look at you. Say the sound it makes as it stands, then turn it and say the other.

outside.title: The Twig Alphabet
paras: The hedges have been dropping twigs all week. Collect a bundle, snap them to matching lengths on the edge of a wall, and lay letters flat on a bare patch of path. Stick to the straight letters: A, Z, L, N, T and E. Build her whole name if the twigs hold out, photograph it, and leave it there.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, so he arrives at the finished letter and walks straight through it. Build his K a little way off and give him three twigs of his own. He collects, drops and collects again.

second.title: The Alphabet You Lie Down In
second.intro: Push the furniture back and charge the phone.
steps: Lie down first and make an L yourself, legs straight, one arm out. Let her stand over you and look at it.
Her turn. Start with the ones a body does on its own: L, T, X, I, and O curled up.
Hold the hand mirror above her while she is in the shape. She sees what she made and adjusts her own arm.
Photograph each one from standing, straight down over her.
Lay the jump rope in a curve for the letters her body will not bend into, a C or an S, and have her lie inside it.
Roll the two dish towels for the strokes she has no limbs left for: the crossbar of an A, the dot above an i. One each.
Scroll back through the lot at the end and let her name them. Anything she gets wrong goes back on the floor.
second.tip: Stop at six letters while she still wants more.

alternatives: Two letters only, hers and yours.
Make the letters with hands and fingers instead.
Chalk the letters on the patio and stand inside them.
Draw the shapes her body made onto paper afterwards.
outAgain: The pet store and the garden center, reading the labels on the tanks
The garden center café if the rain has come in
A thrift store, for a bag of board books
The park, for the leaves that came down this week
A drive somewhere with one big sign to read from the car
days.krestonPM: Build his letter around him with the rope while he is on his back. He gets up and leaves halfway through, so take the photo early. At the pet store, stand him at the fish tanks.

insight.headline: "Different" and "wrong" are separate ideas, and this week teaches the difference.
paras: Azlyn has spent three years learning that a cup stays a cup whichever way it faces. She turns it, drops it, sees it upside down, and the name holds. Letters break that rule, and b and d are one shape facing two ways with two different sounds. Her reversals are the old rule still doing its job, which makes them evidence of good learning. In most children, reversals stay ordinary in writing until around seven. Name the sound the letter makes as it stands, turn it, name the other, and she gets the information without collecting the idea that she is bad at this.

days.safety: Card strips, paper-plate curves and poster putty are all mouth-sized for a 15-month-old who is fast on his feet. Work on the tray, sweep the offcuts back into it between rounds, and keep the tray on the table rather than the floor. Count the putty back into the pack when you finish. The rope comes up off the floor and the mirror goes on a shelf the moment the photographs are done. A loose cord at Kreston's height is a strangulation risk.

days.title: Throwing at the Sounds
days.prepTonight: Dig five odd socks out of the wash, stand them by the rice with a mug, and drag the biggest cardboard box you have behind the sofa.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Sound She Has to Hit

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Sock Balls in the Basket

opening.title: Knotting the Sock Balls
opening.need: 5 odd socks · a bag of rice or lentils · 1 mug for scooping.
steps: Sit on the floor with the bag between you. She holds a sock open with both hands and you pour.
Half a mug in each, no more. Any heavier and a ball that hits somebody hurts.
Knot the top twice and hand it over to be squeezed. Five of them, squeeze-tested, stacked against the wall until 9:15.

main.title: The Sound She Has to Hit
materials: 5 odd socks filled with rice or lentils and knotted
6 sheets of paper, or the cardboard letters from Friday
A clear wall or the back of the sofa
steps: Write one letter big on each sheet in marker: her five, plus an S. If Friday's painted letters are still up, use those and write the S on a single sheet.
Tape them to the wall in a row at her chest height, a hand's width apart.
Stand her two big steps back, close enough to hit something in the first minute.
Call the sound rather than the name. Zzzz. She throws. She misses. Say the sound again, hand her the next ball, say nothing else.
All five balls, then she collects them off the floor and you go again. Twenty throws before you change a single thing.
Once she is hitting, move her line back a step, or call two sounds and ask for them in order.
main.tip: Do not coach her arm. A child being corrected between throws stops throwing.

outside.title: Buckeyes on the Chalk Letters
paras: The horse chestnuts have started dropping. Find one and let her fill her pockets from underneath it, then chalk three big letters on a flat bit of path and let her lob a buckeye at whichever one you call. Rolling counts and so does sliding. Bring a bag home for the windowsill, and check her pockets before the coat goes on the hook.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months. Buckeyes are the wrong size for him, so give him a fat wet leaf to carry. Indoors, sit him in the highchair with one sock ball to drop over the side. He drops it, watches it land and looks at you to fetch it.

second.title: Five Holes and Five Letters
second.intro: The box from behind the sofa only accepts what goes through the hole.
materials: 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
steps: Stand the box on its side, open face to the room. Cut five holes across the front, each wider than a sock ball. She stands well back, and the knife goes straight onto the shelf.
Give her the marker. She marks a letter above each hole in her own version of it, and you write the same letter small in the corner so you can both read it later.
Tape a throwing line on the floor two big steps out from the box.
Call a sound. She posts a ball through that hole. Through counts, off the front does not.
One clothespin on the box rim for every ball in. Eight pegs is the whole game.
Reaching in and fishing the balls back out is her job, not yours.
Once she has cleared the clothespins twice, turn the box round, let her call the sounds and let her watch you miss.
second.tip: Cut the holes bigger than feels right. She should be posting balls inside two minutes, and you can tape a hole half shut when it gets too easy.

alternatives: Throw into the laundry basket, no letters.
Roll the balls at the wall letters.
Mail the balls behind the sofa and fish them out.
Draw round the box and give it a letter for a mouth.
outAgain: The scooter, with a chalk letter at each end of the run
The balance bike on the flat stretch by the pond
A leaf-kicking walk, wherever they have started to pile against a wall
Back for more buckeyes, with a bag this time
The park, for the swings and nothing else
days.krestonPM: Once she has finished with the box, sit him in front of it and let him push a sock ball through the lowest hole. On the scooter run he runs a stretch of it beside her and then wants carrying.

insight.headline: Aiming improves with quantity, not instruction.
paras: Throwing well is a whole-body problem. Her feet, her hips, her shoulder and her release all have to arrive in the right order, and none of that is available to her as words. She solves it by throwing, watching where it went, and adjusting on the next one. Fifty throws beats any coaching, and a wall with letters on it is what buys you fifty. Vary the distance rather than repeating the same spot each time. A body that has thrown from four distances has learned the rule, and a body that has thrown fifty times from one place has learned one throw.

days.safety: Loose rice and lentils are the size Kreston chokes on at 15 months, so the socks get filled with him in the highchair and the floor gets swept before he is down on it. A thrown sock ball finds his head at exactly his height. Keep Kreston behind the throwing line or in the highchair with his own sock ball while she throws, and set the target wall away from where he plays. Buckeyes are a choking hazard and they go in a pocket or a bag, never in his hands. The craft knife is adult-only and goes back out of reach between cuts.

days.title: The Sound Bag
days.prepTonight: Stand four mixing bowls and the marker on the kitchen table, hang a paper bag on the banister, and find two shoeboxes with lids.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Quiet Corner and One Story

opening.title: One Thing From Every Room
steps: Hand her the bag and walk her round the house. One thing out of every room, nothing smaller than her own fist and nothing breakable.
Say the name of each thing as it drops in, with the front of it held long. Sssspoon. Bbbbrush.
Tip the bag onto the table and count what she got. Top it up to twelve out of the kitchen drawer if she came home light.

main.title: Three Bowls, Three Sounds
materials: 12 household objects, all fist-sized or bigger
4 mixing bowls or shoeboxes, one of them Kreston's
steps: Look at the twelve and pick three sounds they cover between them. In most kitchens s, b and c will carry eight of the twelve on their own.
Write one letter on each card in marker and stand a card in front of each bowl.
Hold up an object and say its name with the front stretched out. Sssspoon. Ask her which bowl.
She drops it in, right or wrong. Say the sound of the bowl she chose and the sound of the object one after the other, then move on without fixing it.
Work through all twelve. The odd ones out can sit on the table until the end.
Tip each bowl back out and go through it with her, one object at a time. Finish with her holding things up and you guessing, and get one wrong.
main.tip: Sounds, never letter names. A three-year-old taught see for the letter c has to unlearn it before she can read the word cat.

outside.title: Everything That Starts With S
paras: Take the paper bag out again and hunt one sound down the street. Late September hands you sticks, stones, seeds, slugs after the rain and spider webs strung across every gate. The same orb weavers she counted on the fences two weeks ago are still out there, and bigger. Sky and sun count even though they will not go in the bag. Say each find back to her with the s held long.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food, so bowls and objects together are an invitation he cannot refuse. Give him a fourth bowl of his own and two of the twelve, and he will fill and tip it out for five or ten minutes at a stretch, then come back to it twice more before lunch. He is running her sorting game, minus the sounds.

second.title: Two Boxes, One Choice
second.intro: Two shoeboxes on the table, one you can see into and one you cannot, and twenty pegs on the line to win.
materials: 1 dish towel to cover the second box
1 sheet of paper for the score line
steps: Mark the boxes 1 and 2 with the marker. Box one sits open in front of her. Box two goes to the far end of the table under the dish towel.
Say the rule once, in her words. Box one always pays one peg. Box two pays three pegs or nothing.
Fix your own rule and hold to it: an object from this morning goes into box two on three rounds out of every five. She never sees which.
She picks. Box one: she takes the peg that is always there. Box two: she lifts the lid herself, and an object means three pegs, an empty box means none.
Draw a line down the sheet of paper. Every peg she wins gets laid on the line, so the score is a picture instead of a number.
Ten rounds. Ask her which box she is picking and why, and write down what she says without arguing with any of it.
Last two rounds, she runs the boxes and you pick. She hides an object badly and tells you where it is.
second.tip: Do not steer her towards the safe box or the risky one, and do not tell her which was the better bet at the end. She makes ten of these in a row and watches all ten land.

alternatives: One box and a coin toss, and stop there.
Hide an object under one of three cups.
Sort this morning's twelve objects by size.
Clip the clothespins round the rim of a bowl and count them off.
outAgain: The duck pond, with a tub of defrosted peas or rolled oats
The riverside path, for the leaves coming down along the water
The neighborhood park while the light holds
A slow lap of the block naming everything that starts with s
The garden and a bucket, if the rain has set back in
days.krestonPM: At the pond he goes in the stroller or with a hand in yours the whole time. He is 15 months, he runs, and the edge of the water is the one place that costs you the second you look away. Sit down with him well back and give him a handful of oats to throw from your lap.

insight.headline: Risk and reward is a new kind of decision.
paras: Three is about when Azlyn starts weighing a sure small thing against an uncertain bigger one, and she does it with almost none of the machinery an adult brings. She cannot hold a probability in her head, so she runs on the last outcome: box two paid three pegs, so box two is the good box, and one empty lid flips her back the other way. Watching ten choices land in a row gives her the start of a pattern nobody can explain to her in words. Resist telling her the answer. The clothespins on the line teach it better than a sentence from you would.

days.safety: Never let Kreston loose at the pond edge. A hand or the stroller from the moment the water is in sight, and the same again on the walk back. The clothespins are mouth-sized for him, springs and all, so they stay up on the table between rounds and go back in the bag at the end. Keep the shoebox lids off the floor, and put the twelve objects away when the sorting stops rather than leaving them down there for a 15-month-old at a run.

days.title: The Sound She Turns Into
days.prepTonight: Stand the cornstarch by the food coloring with two saucers and a teaspoon, and put out an old T-shirt she can ruin.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Paint You Can Put on Skin

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Animal That Starts With Her Sound

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Book About the Animal She Was

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Story She Told, Read Back

opening.title: The Paint You Can Put on Skin
opening.need: 2 tbsp cornstarch · 1 tbsp water · 1 tsp lotion · food coloring · 2 saucers · 1 teaspoon.
steps: Cornstarch and water into a saucer, and she stirs it smooth with the teaspoon. It goes stiff, then loose.
Stir the lotion through until it stops looking floury, split it between the two saucers and drop a color into each.
Dab a spot on the inside of her arm and one on yours. Leave both while you clear the table, and ask which animal she wants to be.

main.title: The Animal That Starts With Her Sound
materials: 1 soft small brush or a handful of cotton swabs
steps: The saucers from the opening hold the mixture. Check the test patch. Red or raised, and it stops here: wipe it with the wet washcloth and use crayons instead.
Ask her for a sound she likes and an animal that starts with it. Zebra for the z in her name, or bear, cat, snake.

Towel round her shoulders, her facing you. Big shapes first with the brush: a muzzle, a band across the nose, a color over each cheek. Cotton swabs for the whiskers and stripes, two minutes and no more.
Hand her the hand mirror and say nothing while she looks.
She is that animal until half past two. Use its name, ask it questions, let it eat snack off the floor. Photograph her at 10:00 for this afternoon.
main.tip: Paint yourself as well, even one stripe.

outside.title: Prowling Through the Leaves
paras: The leaves along the path edges are down in drifts now. She goes out as the animal you painted on her this morning and moves as it moves: stalking the drifts, freezing behind a wall, pouncing on nothing. Find a hedge she can hide inside and come looking for her. Use her animal's name where other people can hear it.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months, and a painted face on the person who feeds him takes easing into. Let him watch you paint your own stripe, then show him both faces in the mirror. Point at Azlyn and name the animal and he points back.

second.title: The Book About the Animal She Was
second.intro: She has been whatever she chose since half past nine. Before the paint comes off, the animal dictates its morning and you take it down word for word.
materials: 3 sheets of letter-size paper folded and taped into a booklet
1 glue stick or a strip of masking tape
Washable poster paint and 1 wide soft brush
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Fold the three sheets in half together and tape the spine, or run a line of glue. Twelve small pages.
Ask what the animal did this morning. It woke up, it had toast. Write her sentence at the foot of page one in marker, her words and her grammar.
Ask what happened next, write it down, then put the crayons beside her and leave the page with her.
Four or five pages is a whole book. Stop when she stops.
Put your phone in front of her with the 10:00 photo and let her draw her own painted face for the cover.
Read it back with your finger under each word, then again after half past two when the paint has come off.

The September handprint sheet last. Kreston goes on it first while he is calm, the wet washcloth already in your other hand. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write September, his 15 months and her 3 beside the two prints.
second.tip: Put no mark on the pages yourself except the words she gives you.

alternatives: One page and one sentence, and call it a book.
Draw the animal on a paper plate as a mask.
Act the story out instead.
outAgain: Swimming, with the face washed off before you leave
The pool's quiet session if the main one is full
Indoor playground, for a body that has been prowling since half past ten
Straight home, if the pool has taken everything she had
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool. At 15 months he walks the steps holding both your hands and would walk straight off the edge on his own. Twenty minutes in, then out and dressed before he is cold.

insight.headline: A painted face changes behavior as well as appearance.
paras: Give Azlyn a character to be and she gets access to a version of herself with more patience in it. Researchers ran this with four-year-olds asked to stick at a dull task as Batman, and the ones in character lasted longer. The distance does the work: the animal she picked can wait, can be brave in a hedge, can try the thing Azlyn would refuse. Would a zebra put its shoes on? is the kind of question that lands where a straight instruction has been bouncing off since breakfast. The paint comes off at bath time and the trick outlasts it by a couple of years.

days.safety: Test the mixture on the inside of her arm first. Nothing goes on broken skin, near her eyes or on her lips. Food coloring stains skin as well as clothes, so two drops rather than ten and an old T-shirt. Check how the arm patch comes off before any of it goes near her face. Keep the saucers off the floor and out of Kreston's reach; at 15 months he will taste anything the color of pudding. At the pool, stay within an arm's length of both of them the whole time, and Kreston is never on the side on his own. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Her Name in Five Pieces
days.prepTonight: Put a sheet of thick card and the marker on the table, and cut a thumbnail-sized window in a second piece of card.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Library Books on the Rug

opening.title: Cutting the Name Apart
opening.need: 1 sheet of thick card · 1 permanent marker · 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only) · 1 tray.
steps: Write AZLYN across the card in big capitals, well spaced, with her watching each letter go down.
Read it back with her finger under each one, then cut between the letters while she holds the far edge still. The scissors stay in your hand and go on the shelf after the last cut.
Five loose cards on the tray. Let her push them about and get them back in order however she manages. Leave the tray until 9:15.

main.title: Putting the Name Back Together
materials: 4 sheets of thick card or cereal-box card, one per name
Scissors (adult only, used in the opening and again in steps 4 and 5)
4 paper strips with the family's names written out as models
steps: Write the four names on the four paper strips in marker: AZLYN, JOSEPH, BROOKLYN, KRESTON. Lay hers along the top of the tray and scatter her five cards below it, out of order.
She rebuilds it against the model, matching shapes rather than reading. Put your finger under the first letter and wait her out.
Do it again with the model face down. She will place two and ask for it back. Turn it over the second she asks.
Write JOSEPH big across a fresh sheet and cut it apart the same way, her holding the card and you holding the scissors. Lay his strip as the model.
BROOKLYN and KRESTON if she is still with you. Both are a stretch, so sit alongside and put your finger where the next letter goes.
Line all four rebuilt names down the tray and read them out. Ask her whose is longest, then count the letters along each.
main.tip: Hers is the one she does alone. Sit shoulder to shoulder for the other three and help before she asks.

outside.title: The Street Sign Hunt
paras: Walk the street reading it. Capital letters out here are bigger than anything indoors: road signs, house numbers, the side of a van, the mailbox, a license plate. Hunt her five and call each one out. Low autumn sun makes some signs unreadable from one sidewalk, so cross over at the corner and try from the shade.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at pictures in books, and out here he points at everything. Give him the word for whatever his finger lands on, then add the first sound of it on its own.

second.title: The Letter Window
second.intro: A rectangle the size of a thumbnail, cut in card, shows her one letter at a time.
materials: 1 piece of card with a small window cut in it
Torn paper scraps to mark the pages
steps: Show her what it does first. Lay the card flat on a page and slide it until one letter fills the window. Say that letter's sound.
Hand the card over. She slides it wherever she likes and you say the sound of whatever lands in the frame.
Now hunt. Pick her A and go looking. She slides the window along a line and stops when she thinks she has one.
Every A she finds earns a mark on the notepad, one straight line in marker, her hand and not yours.
Any page with a lot of them gets a torn scrap laid in. She comes back to those.
Change the letter. Save the Z until last, because she will hunt a whole book before it turns up.
Count the marks together at the end and say each sound out loud as she counts.
second.tip: Hold the book still and let her move the card.

alternatives: Use the window on a cereal box or a magazine.
Cut a bigger window and hunt whole words.
Read the books and leave the card in the drawer.
Draw round the window on paper and fill each frame.
outAgain: The library, and let her find her letter down the spines on the bottom shelf
Indoor playground, if the story session has filled the place
The park on the way home, for the last of the afternoon light
The thrift store next door, for a bag of board books
Straight home with the new books
days.krestonPM: Put him down in the board-book corner and let him pull things off the low shelf. At 15 months he points at pictures, so sit behind him and name whatever he lands on. He hands his own board book up to the person at the desk, which he could not have managed a month ago.

insight.headline: Building it back up is the part that's doing the work.
paras: Taking her name apart costs Azlyn nothing. She scatters five cards and the job is done. Putting it back asks her to hold an order in her head, check it against a model, and notice that the third card belongs in the fourth place, and that is the work reading wants from her later. Children remember a sequence they have reassembled better than one they watched somebody else assemble. Scatter the cards more often than feels useful. Every rebuild is another run at the same order, and the fifth is quicker than the first because she is starting to keep it.

days.safety: You do every cut and she holds the card still. The scissors go back on the shelf between cuts and never leave your hand. The loose letter cards are mouth-sized for a 15-month-old, so the tray stays up on the table whenever Kreston is loose in the room. Reading the street means her head is up and her feet are moving: walk the house side of the sidewalk with yourself between both children and the traffic, cross at the corner with a hand held, and keep Kreston in the stroller with the brake on whenever you stop to read something.

days.title: Letters You Can Eat
days.prepTonight: Leave 1½ sticks of butter out to soften overnight, cut three arm's-lengths of string, and clear the middle oven shelf.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Three Parcels That Have to Last

opening.title: Rubbing In the Butter
opening.need: 2 cups all-purpose flour (250 g) · 6 tbsp superfine sugar (75 g) · 1½ sticks softened butter (175 g) · 1 mixing bowl · 1 plate for the fridge.
steps: Flour and sugar into the bowl. She stirs it with a whole hand rather than a spoon.
Butter in, torn into lumps. Rub it through your fingers together until the bowl looks like damp sand, a good ten minutes.
Squeeze the lot into one ball, onto the plate and into the fridge until 9:15. Cold dough holds a letter; warm dough spreads.

main.title: A Cookie for Every Initial
steps: The ball from the fridge is 2 cups all-purpose flour, 6 tbsp superfine sugar and 1½ sticks of softened butter, rubbed together and chilled. Oven on at 325°F, tray lined with baking paper.

Flour the board. Cut the dough into four with the table knife and hand her the first piece. She rolls it under both flat hands into a rope as thick as her finger; a stubborn lump gets the rolling pin.
Bend the rope into a letter on the tray. B for Brooklyn, J for Joseph, A for Azlyn, K for Kreston. Say whose it is as it goes down.

Trim the overshooting ends with the table knife and press every join hard, or the letter comes out of the oven in pieces. Lay the trimmings in a short line of their own on the tray and bake them with the letters; that line is Kreston's, and it saves the four.
Fifteen to eighteen minutes, until pale gold and no darker. Slide the paper onto the wire rack and leave them until stone cold; a warm letter breaks in her hand.
main.tip: A slim K has three thin arms that snap between tray and plate. Roll the ropes thick.

outside.title: Water Letters on the Fence
paras: Fill a bucket, take the widest brush in the house out to the fence and let her paint letters two feet tall on the panels. They come up dark, hold a minute and fade from the top down as the wood dries, so she works fast and starts again. Late September wood is damp, so hers last.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and wet is his favorite thing. Give him a brush and two inches of water in a cup and he will paint one patch of fence for five or ten minutes, then come back to it twice. Hold him up to the wire rack first and point at the K.

second.title: Three Parcels That Have to Last
second.intro: Four cookies came out of the oven and one is hers. The other three have to survive on a shelf until six.
materials: 1 ball of string, three arm's-lengths cut off it
1 tin or box with a lid
steps: Lay the four cookies out and let her eat hers in front of the other three. Those three are for tonight and she is in charge of them.
One sheet of paper per parcel and one spare. She covers them in crayon while you say whose each is. Write the name big across the top in permanent marker and she copies the first letter underneath.
Fold the paper round a cookie and tape the seams. Her folding is terrible and the tape covers it.
Tie a cut length of string round each parcel. She holds a finger on the cross while you pull the knot tight.
All three into the tin, lid on, and the tin on a high shelf she can see and not reach.
Six o'clock, she gets the tin down with you and hands each parcel to the right person. Kreston's gets opened for him.
second.tip: She will want to check the tin over and over. Let her.

alternatives: One parcel, hers, and everybody eats the rest now.
Draw a card for each person instead.
Mail the parcels through the doors with Friday's letters.
Hide the tin and draw a map to it.
outAgain: The bakery, to look at what has letters iced on it
The grocery store, and she finds an A on three boxes
The park while the light lasts, which is going fast now
The post office, to send one of Friday's drawings
Straight home, if the tin on the shelf is all she can think about
days.krestonPM: Break him a crumb off the baked trimmings from step 4, and leave the parcels in the tin. At 15 months he is spooning his own food and a shortbread crumb is well within him. At the bakery, hold him up to the glass and name the tray he points at.

insight.headline: Saving three of something is harder than it sounds.
paras: Azlyn holding back three cookies for eight hours is doing something her brain is not built for yet. Waiting sits at the front of the brain and hers has years of building left, so willpower is the wrong thing to ask her for. Scaffolding works, and today carries three pieces of it: the cookies go out of sight in a tin, the wrapping turns them into somebody else's property, and the job you gave her makes waiting an achievement rather than a deprivation. Children who manage this are the ones handed good structure, and you built her some of it this afternoon.

days.safety: The oven is on through the middle of the morning and Kreston runs at 15 months. Say it out loud each time either comes near, keep him out of the kitchen while the tray moves, and cool the tray on a high surface rather than the table. Stay within arm's reach of him for every minute the bucket holds water and tip it out the moment she stops painting the fence. A bucket at Kreston's height is a drowning risk even at two inches. Raw dough is not for eating, by anyone. Keep the cut string on the table and the ball in the drawer; loose cord at his height is a strangulation risk.
